items.title: Reddit Will Force Everyone to Log In
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Reddit plans to require users to log in to browse the platform, ending its longstanding practice of allowing anonymous visitors to access posts and discussions. According to CEO Steve Huffman, a key reason behind the decision is to curb unauthorized scraping and automated traffic.
 
"This is a big change for Reddit, where we've allowed logged-out access to basically all of Reddit for the last two decades," Huffman says. "And I don't know about you, but as someone whose life has been defined by the open internet, it's a big change for me. But I've come to the conclusion that this is the right decision for our platform and the right decision for our business." The Verge reports: There's no definitive timeline on when this change will roll out to all users, or how the site will work if you're logged out. (If I send my friend a link to a thread and they aren't logged in, what will they see?) To start, Reddit will test the logged-in requirement in "select markets outside the US" in the "coming months," according to CEO Steve Huffman. "We'll look at the impact on the user experience, on our business, and on the whole Reddit ecosystem, figure out where the right boundaries are, and go from there." Reddit has also rebuilt and is rereleasing the Reddit app's incognito mode.
 
Huffman claims the login requirement is better for Reddit's user experience and its ads business and is "more protective of Reddit data." The "vast majority" of unauthorized Reddit access happens "through our logged-out experiences," though the company will still strike licensing deals of its data with companies, like the deals it made with OpenAI and Google in 2024. Huffman notes that Reddit does not need to know a logged-in user's identity -- "Honestly, we don't want to know" -- just that the user is logged in at all. And he says that more logged-in users lets the company deliver "more relevant ads."

items.title: Binance Suffers Biggest Crypto Hack In History With $6.3 Billion Affected [UPDATE]
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
UPDATE 10/30/26: Binance has temporarily suspended customer withdrawals after suffering what investigators say is the biggest crypto hack in history. According to Binance CEO Yi He, the company estimates roughly $6.3 billion in funds were impacted, with roughly $3 billion in assets frozen on-chain so far. Rest assured, "your money is safe, and we're covering every loss," said co-CEO Richard Teng in a LinkedIn post.
 
"This was a complex attack," said Teng. "The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and tracers, making it more difficult for us to trace." From a report: Teng said the incident was not carried out by one person. While the initial investigation indicated the involvement of a compromised laptop, further digging revealed additional points of breach. [...] Blockchain analysis firms TRM Labs and Elliptic have linked the theft to North Korean hackers, with TRM attributing it "with high confidence" to a group known as TraderTraitor, the same group responsible for last year's Bybit hack.
 
Elliptic estimated Friday that about 44% of the stolen assets have been frozen, with stablecoins accounting for nearly all of those funds. The firm estimated that attackers still controlled over $3 billion in crypto that token issuers cannot directly freeze.
 
The hackers appear to have compromised Binance's wallet-signing infrastructure, allowing them to authorize transactions that drained billions of dollars in cryptocurrency across multiple blockchains, according to the firms. Binance, in its preliminary stage, has conducted an investigation into the hack, which suggests the incident may have begun with a compromised engineer's laptop. The exchange added that it has found no evidence that wallet passwords were leaked. Below is the original story from yesterday, Oct. 29th. 
Binance is investigating a potential hack after more than $2 billion in crypto was drained from one of its wallets into a new external account, with Blockaid estimating nearly $3.3 billion was moved.
 
"Our teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating," said Binance on X.
 
"User funds are safe," said Binance founder CZ. "It does look like a hack on Binance. Appreciate the quick freeze from Tether (~$971m) and Circle (~$823m). I don't manage Binance anymore, but as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."
 
At around the same time, crypto-based prediction market Polymarket reported its own security incident that wiped out around $2.7 million in user funds.

items.title: The Tragedy of Losing Your Wikipedia Page
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes an excerpt from a Wired article that explores the often-contentious process of nominating pages for deletion when their subjects fail to meet the encyclopedia's notability standards: What do you need to know -- need to know -- about Xavier Trudeau? The eldest son of former Canadian prime minister Justin, the teenage Trudeau has recently begun performing R&B under the mononym Xav. But, with all due respect to Xav, do those facts make him a person of note? Should you expect to be able to read about him on Wikipedia? What about Evanescence guitarist Tim McCord, or 2012 Yachtmaster of the Year Rainer Holtorff? All three have had a biography on Wikipedia; all three of those biographies were considered for deletion this year on the grounds that the subjects were not notable enough to warrant a biography at all. Every day, dozens, sometimes hundreds, of Wikipedia biographies -- of child actors turned LA realtors, retired ambassadors, soccer players who have played less than 10 minutes of professional soccer -- are purged from the world's free encyclopedia.
 
It's not as though Wikipedia, which hosts over 7 million articles in the English language, doesn't have the space. But Wikipedia has only so many volunteers to monitor its contents. To this day, Wikipedia editors are discovering hoaxes that have gone undetected for decades. The time it takes to verify the release dates of Xav's three singles is better spent -- the logic goes -- by asking whether the American Civil War officer Nathaniel Lyon really drank mustard during battle, as was claimed in his Wikipedia biography for 17 years. Wikipedia removed the mustard claim, not because it was proven wrong, but because there was no reliable evidence for it. "We're not really looking for what's true," Britta Gustafson, who has been editing Wikipedia since 2001, told me. "We're looking for what's verifiable." Wikipedia editors do not themselves decide that a person is not notable, only that there is a lack of reliable evidence to support the claim...

items.title: Apple Is Entering Its Slop Era
items.author: Matthew Gault
items.content:
The once dominant company is struggling to find its feet in an AI-driven post-Tim Cook world. John Ternus — a 25 year veteran of the company with a track record of pushing harebrained hardware schemes like the and butterfly keyboard. 

With Ternus at the helm, I feel there’s a good chance Apple’s best days are behind it, that it will have to make do with less, that it’s déclassé. Apple, blindsided by AI and relying on crowdpleasing hardware gimmicks, is downwardly mobile. It’s in its slop era. The company that once asked consumers to is now releasing hardware that’s just like everything else on the market.

Apple is not adjusting to this new position well. AI boosters agree that Siri AI is awful. Apple HomeView is a $300 Apple Watch meant to replace the family hearth. The iPhone Duo has only been out for a few days and all people can talk about is the cracks, yet Ternus is on the cover of Time Magazine this week holding the folding iPhone Duo and staring at the camera. “The other examples in the world felt kind of cheap and crappy,” . Many people holding cracked iPhone Duos this week are learning just what (not) cheap and crappy looks like.

Flailing from crackgate, Apple announced the launch of a touch-screen laptop, an idea Steve Jobs extensively tested and ,” an idea Cook once compared to combining a toaster with a refrigerator. What’s next? What if the toaster-refigerator folded? Ternus has been trying to make an 18-inch foldable iPad . Maybe Apple will solve the screen cracking issues by then. Or maybe Ternus will continue to try to put .

I have been waiting for this moment for more than a decade. I am relishing Apple’s recent trajectory more than I should. I confess I harbor a secret and petty grudge.

In 2010, when Apple released the iPhone 4 I was working as a floor manager at a Banana Republic in Dallas. I was interested in smart phones, of course, but Dallas is an expensive city and the iPhone was a luxury. I made do . But the suit-wearing middle management retail psychopaths that were my coworkers saw my lack of an iPhone as a weakness. It was not, as they say now, On Brand.

I had started at the store in the stock room, working my way up to manage the backroom before ascending to a coveted position on the sales floor. The other managers made it clear that a Razr was a “backroom” phone and someone in a prominent position on the floor needed to be seen using an iPhone.

At first, I was not to buy an iPhone. The message came in the form of subtle and not so subtle bullying deployed over weeks.

“Still using that old phone?” they’d say.“Didn’t you get a raise?” someone would ask a week later.

“Try not to use that on the sales floor,” one co-worker told me, pointing at my Razr. “We’re trying to project a certain image here.”

The social pressure had the opposite of its intended effect. I resisted. Eventually one of the friendlier managers pulled me aside. He told me that my colleagues thought it was weird that I didn't have an iPhone. He said I needed to buy one to fit in and he said the store could give me an advance on my paycheck to make it happen.

Ever the contrarian and pissed I was experiencing high school style bullying as a full grown adult, I threw in with Google instead. I got an . My coworkers weren’t happy, but they stopped bringing up the iPhone. 

I’ve been an Android user ever since and studiously avoided Apple products until I broke down a few years ago and bought a Macbook Air. Time heals all wounds and Windows laptops are garbage. I’d even been considering changing from Android to iPhone because the privacy features are more robust. I’ve never been averse to a fast food meal either and maybe I’m a little more comfortable with Apple now that the cracks are starting to show in the foldable phone.

items.title: The Trump Admin Isn’t Bright Enough To ‘Ban’ Foreign Robots And Drones, And The Press Should Stop Pretending Otherwise
items.author: Karl Bode
items.content:
Ideally, I think it makes sense to open up the U.S. market to Chinese goods (AI, EVs, robots), but have functional and well-funded regulators that police all labor, competition, environmental, privacy, national security, and consumer rights abuses. But big U.S. companies because it would boost competition regulatory accountability, eroding quarterly revenues.

So instead we get corruption-fueled protectionism run by a bunch of racist, and incompetent clowns who gutted most of our federal regulators, then saddled them with an elaborate new policy ask that’s impossible to implement, even if the admin .

For example, I recommend this recent Verge piece about the Trump effort to ban Chinese drones, which notes how it has been trivial for Chinese companies to trick the administration and bypass the ban simply by renting a strip mall office, tweaking a few names, and pretending their equipment is produced domestically. Curiously, officials who don’t believe in government can’t govern. Fancy that.

Another report this week by Ars Technica indicates that U.S. chip giant Intel has also been so disoriented and confused they felt it necessary to get a waiver from the Trump administration’s “foreign robot ban” because executives didn’t really understand what is or isn’t covered:

“Intel’s waiver request stated that it was “unclear” whether its robotic vehicles even qualify as robots covered by the FCC ban but said it sought relief just in case. The tech company also received approval to “make certain hardware, software, and firmware changes” that would help ensure the continued operation and maintenance of the robotic vehicles.”

So it’s a foreign robot ban, unless we need foreign robots. In which case big U.S. companies have to spend a bunch of time and money kissing the Trump administration’s ass to ensure they have what they need to function. It’s far from the “free market” dogma the administration rose to power on. It’s a weird and racist autocratic nanny state operated by the dimmest people imaginable.

A recent study by the International Data Corporation predicts that the foreign robot ban could reduce US humanoid robot revenues by 58 percent over expected baseline. China is still expected to dominate the market with most of its cheaper, better gear avoiding the U.S. for the EU. And much like the FCC “drone ban,” a big impact will be less tech product availability and higher prices overall for U.S. consumers.

The Trump administration makes an endless stink about protecting U.S. cybersecurity defenses by taking aim at Chinese-made tech. But with its other hand it has devastated U.S. cybersecurity agencies with policies that are indistinguishable from a foreign attack, make it easier for foreign governments to surveil U.S. citizens at scale (the refusal to pass real privacy laws or regulate data brokers, for example), and function largely as a way for the administration to line its own pockets.

Again, protectionism is bad. But what we have here . There’s zero real indication that the Trump administration has any idea what it’s doing. There’s simply no reality in which the Trump administration can implement or enforce any of this. And because our consolidated corporate press sucks, most coverage simply refuses to make this clear to anybody.

Outlets like Reuters, for example, inform the public that the Trump administration is “aiming to safeguard the U.S. artificial intelligence supply chain from Chinese threats.” Others will parrot claims that the Trump administration is “dedicated to creating safety guardrails for AI.” But there’s no real evidence that’s true or that the administration is capable of doing literally any of that.

This sort of pseudo-journalism will be all the rage in the new year as the Trump administration sets its sights on a likely ban of foreign AI models (to lock in the dominance of U.S. giants that dutifully kiss the authoritarian ring). Which is to say: expect this sort of normalization and sanewashing to despite zero evidence that of this is working or makes any coherent sense.

items.title: Proton CEO Is In 'Full AI Psychosis'
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
According to 404 Media, Proton CEO Andy Yen is aggressively pushing AI adoption while fostering what workers describe as a culture of fear that discourages raising security concerns or challenging leadership. The investigation is based on interviews with eight current and one former Proton employees, as well as internal Slack chats, meeting recordings, and an AI manifesto written by the company's CTO. Longtime Slashdot reader devnulljapan summarizes the findings: Engineers at Proton, which makes the encrypted email service Proton Mail and a suite of privacy- and security-focused products, including an encrypted drive service, an authenticator app, and a password manager, are being pushed to "stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more." Workers describe an environment where employees have genuine concerns about security or being asked to develop security products with AI but feel unable to voice them, lest Yen berates them in front of everyone or threatens their employment at the company. "The CEO is in full AI psychosis and has been for a while now," one of the sources told 404 Media. Yen reportedly dismissed an employee's request for additional security testing before releasing new code, calling it "bullshit and loser thinking" and insisting that "only losers think like that." In a separate exchange over Proton's post-quantum encryption rollout, Yen criticized how the company communicated the feature's limitations and told employees that "perception is more important than truth, the truth doesn't matter if you don't win on perception."
 
"The train is coming, get onboard or get crushed. Don't be the professional fax machine operator in the internet age," Yen wrote to the security Slack channel. "I think by the end of this year most developers stop programming and start writing specs for tests that AI will code and run, to validate AI written code that humans will no longer be able to review. This will be the last year that we hire engineers, and starting next year we hire what we used to call product managers, to build things with AI."

A third-party vendor based in the United Kingdom was breached, not the prediction market's website itself. Law enforcement in the UK have been notified of the incident, the company said. Trading was initially paused while the company investigated for several hours.
 
On X, prominent traders complained that they had lost money; Blockchain analytics firm Bubblemaps reported that around 700 users appear affected, with approximately $2.7 million stolen. Polymarket declined to comment when WIRED asked how many traders were impacted by the breach and how much money was lost, but said it will refund impacted traders.
 
The hack did not impact users on Polymarket US, the company's newer platform for people within the United States. Polymarket runs two separate prediction markets; Polymarket US operates as a federally regulated financial exchange within the country, while the flagship Polymarket is a cryptocurrency-based platform that is banned in the United States and a number of other countries. This is not the first time that Polymarket traders have experienced losses like this. "A nearly identical vendor-compromise attack hit the platform in June, draining close to $3 million from at least 11 user wallets through the same kind of injected frontend script," reports StartupFortune.
 
Hours before Polymarket halted trading, more than $2 billion in cryptocurrency was drained from Binance wallets in just 40 minutes.

items.title: Study: America’s Measles Problem Is Domestic, Not RFK Jr.’s Dirty Foreigners
items.author: Timothy Geigner
items.content:
To state that RFK Jr. says things that are just plainly wrong is to state the obvious. His waffling claims about the dangers of vaccines are wrong. His various other pet conspiracy theories, such as chemtrails and damage to humans from EMF, are also wrong. The data HHS is putting out under his leadership about how many measles deaths have occurred this year is also wrong. Hell, at a recent campaign event in Michigan, a state with a large Arab population, Kennedy decided that the best way to stump for Mike Rogers was to claim that none of the Arabs throughout the world produce any science or literature, which is also wrong.

“There’s 500 million Arabs in the world, and yet they don’t produce science, they don’t win the Nobel Prize, they don’t win the Fields prize, they don’t win the Wolf Prize, they don’t produce literature,” he said.

Arabs have won all those prizes. Peter Hotez, who is a professor at the Baylor College of Medicine and specializes in vaccine development and tropical medicine, said his late colleague, Nobel Prize winner Ahmed Zewail, who was Arab and died in 2016, “would disagree” with Kennedy’s comments.

So, not just wrong, but racist in perhaps the stupidest manner possible given his only reason for being in Michigan in the first place.

So let’s rewind the clock back to April, when Kennedy decided to tell the public that this whole measles outbreak thing had nothing to do with him. Rather, the only reason we had the outbreaks to begin with was because of dirty foreigners coming in as immigrants.

But despite Kennedy being the most vocal source of vaccine misinformation, the secretary tried to blame the outbreaks entirely on immigrants who come to the U.S. from countries where measles is not eliminated — framing the issue as a global epidemic rather than a national public health crisis.

“It has nothing to do with me,” he told lawmakers. “If you’re worried about polio and tuberculosis, you should look at the immigration policies in this country. ’Cause the place where it’s occurring are the place[s] where the immigrants are going, because they’re not vaccinated.”

That was wrong too, of course. We knew it at the time, just was we knew that the practice of blaming immigrants for disease outbreaks is such common practice that we could set our watches to it. But now we have actual data on how the measles is spreading in America and that data fully puts the lie to Kennedy’s bigotry.

Most of the meat of the study focuses on very specific instances in which Washington state endured measles infections that were spread specifically from South Carolina earlier this year.

The study in Washington relied heavily on epidemiological data, linking cases among contacts and exposure sites. But also key to the work was whole-genome sequencing, which made clear that cases didn’t just stem from one single introduction of the virus from South Carolina that then spread among Washington residents; instead, it revealed five separate introductions.

“As public health jurisdictions prepare to respond to increased measles importations linked to domestic measles outbreaks, while remaining vigilant for international importations, timely whole-genome sequencing can supplement epidemiologic information to help differentiate distinct importations from local transmission and inform outbreak response,” the authors conclude.

But when you pair that with the data from CDC as to exactly how the infections are spreading, you get both the micro and macro data for how it’s occurring.

Kennedy claims that there is a “global outbreak” and the US is “doing a better job than any country in the world at controlling the measles outbreak.” Both claims are false. Dozens of other countries have lower case rates than the US. While some countries, including neighboring Canada and Mexico, are also seeing large increases in cases, the soaring case tally in the US is not being driven by international imports, but by domestic spread in under-vaccinated communities.

There can be no doubt that disease is sometimes imported into America from foreign visitors. But the point is that that just isn’t the real problem here. America’s measles problem is a problem, not a matter of immigration. If we had maintained our vaccination rates such that we had herd immunity, we’d be fine.

It’s because of Kennedy’s many, many lies on vaccines that we are not. Don’t let him tell you another lie, that this is all a result of immigrants, to cover up his responsibility.

items.title: Your Diary Has A Creditor: What Character.ai’s Bankruptcy Does To Freedom Of Thought
items.author: Caroline De Cock
items.content:
What is covered by freedom of thought in the AI age is being decided by courts that are hearing cases about something entirely different. The Chapter 11 filing of Character.ai on October 12 is the second such case in a year, and it shows that the record of how a person thought can be produced as evidence, auctioned as an asset or inherited by a buyer, depending on which dispute reaches that record first.

The picture that fits is a diary written on pages that belong to somebody else. The user types into a window that works as a place to think, and the law treats the window as the property of the company that supplied the pages. Nobody asks whether the stationery supplier owes a duty of confidence before protecting a diary, because the diary is protected for what it contains, namely people’s inner thoughts. A chatbot user has no such luck: when the company fails, its creditors can claim whatever the estate holds, and the trustee inventories the notebooks like any other asset.

A U.S. insolvency estate now holds the confidences of millions of users

Character.ai filed for Chapter 11 protection in Delaware and says it will keep operating while a court-supervised process sells the business, with a close expected in late November or early December 2026. Disney is the stalking horse bidder, offering $20 million for a non-exclusive, perpetual license. According to a notice filed by forty U.S. State attorneys general, that license excludes the app, the user data, and the chat content, so the most intimate part of the company stays in the estate unless another bidder wants it. The company’s lawyer told the court that no buyer has yet made an offer for the user data or the chatbot business.

The privacy policy anticipated this moment. It allows chat transcripts, voice recordings, and images to be disclosed in connection with a sale, and it does not require a buyer to follow the original terms and conditions a user signed up for. In its filing, Pennsylvania claims the company had more than 20 million monthly active users, and the Kentucky complaint, cited in the multistate notice, counts more than 2.1 million U.S. accounts with a declared age under 18 out of 21.6 million as of March 2025. The notice furthermore argues that many minors were recorded as adults, as they did not give their actual birth date when creating a profile.

The attorneys general appeared before Judge Brendan Shannon on October 14 to ask that any buyer protect those chat histories. New York Attorney General Letitia James said the company had collected “some of the most private thoughts children have ever shared.” The states reserved the right to seek a consumer privacy ombudsman, an approach that was used in the 23andMe case.

The OpenAI litigation reached the same result through copyright

This is not a phenomenon limited to bankruptcy. Similarly, nobody in the New York Times v OpenAI copyright case launched in 2023 turned freedom of thought into a key element, even if it was raised at the fringes of the debate. In May 2025, the court ordered OpenAI to preserve output logs that would otherwise be deleted, and Sam Altman answered by calling for an “AI privilege,” arguing that talking to an AI should be like talking to a lawyer or a doctor. The duty to preserve new logs ended on September 26, 2025, and excluded logs from requests originating in the European Economic Area, Switzerland and the United Kingdom from continued preservation. On January 5, 2026, Judge Stein affirmed an order to produce 20 million de-identified conversations, finding that the magistrate judge had adequately balanced users’ privacy against the relevance of the documents. In other words, the chat conversations were just business as usual under the logic of ordinary operation of discovery in a U.S. court.

The individual scale followed in February. In United States v. Heppner, Judge Rakoff held that 31 documents a defendant generated with Claude were not privileged, because Claude is not an attorney and the consumer terms defeated any expectation of confidentiality.

Sam Altman and Judge Rakoff disagree on the result but look at the issue from the same perspective: to them, protection depends on what the machine is. Privileges protect relationships between humans and professionals who owe enforceable duties, so a chatbot cannot qualify. In the present bankruptcy case, the point is moot, as privilege only governs what a court may hear. It says nothing about what a company may keep, sell, or hand to a buyer, and that is the question that should be at the core of Character.ai bankruptcy.

Protection has to attach to the act of thinking, not to the file it leaves behind

International human rights law offers two zones. The forum internum, the inner realm of thought, is absolutely protected. The forum externum, the realm of expression, is subject to limitation. The binary was drawn when thinking left no trace and was limited to the inner workings of our brain. In a paper published in July 2026, I propose the creation of a third zone, the forum interstitiale, for external acts that perform the function of thinking, such as a prompt, an abandoned draft and a confession made to a machine. 

Applied to the Character.ai estate, such an approach would guarantee predictability, as the protection would exist before the user types, not after a bankruptcy judge balances interests case by case. 

Bankruptcy procedure handles personal data as a line in a customer list. A diary has no place on that list and a privacy policy cannot supply sufficient safeguards. 

Europe has the same gap and a second way to widen it

Europe should not feel smug about Delaware. The e-Evidence Regulation has applied since August 18, 2026, and providers now have 10 days to answer a European Production Order and 8 hours in an emergency. The rules cover content data and reach services that store or process user data as a defining part of what they offer, a description that includes AI chatbots. A year of conversations with a chatbot is content data. The negotiators of that instrument were not thinking about chatbots, which is the pattern that Delaware and the Southern District of New York have already shown.

The one moment in the OpenAI saga when European residents fared better was the exclusion of requests originating in the European Economic Area. That exemption is, however, triggered by where a request came from and has nothing to say about what the user was doing.

Four rules would stop the diary from becoming an auction lot:

  1. Bankruptcy courts should appoint a consumer privacy ombudsman in the Character.ai case before any bid for the chat logs is considered, and should decline to treat boilerplate sale clauses as consent to transfer the records of users, and especially children’s private thoughts.
  2. Legislators should put one screening question to every AI instrument: what happens to user conversations when the company fails, when a court asks for them and when a regulator pushes the provider to filter them.
  3. Providers should retain less, keep identity data separate from content and offer modes in which nothing readable exists to hand over, so that they can say so truthfully to a court, a trustee or a buyer.
  4. Litigators should argue the functional frame, which asks what the person was doing, and abandon the relational frame, which asks what the machine is.

None of this means that chatbot conversations should be beyond the reach of law. Evidence of wrongdoing may need to be preserved. Allegations of harm to children must be investigated. Legitimate competing interests do not disappear because someone used AI.

But neither should those interests automatically reduce the record of a person’s thinking to an ordinary corporate asset or an unrestricted source of evidence.

The law, in most cases, already understands that a diary deserves protection because of what it contains, not because of who manufactured the notebook. AI conversations require a similar change of perspective.

Caroline De Cock is a communications and policy expert, author, and entrepreneur.

items.title: Court Tosses Trump’s Clumsy Attempt To Scuttle Musk Memphis Data Center Pollution Lawsuit
items.author: Karl Bode
items.content:
Civil rights groups like the Southern Environmental Law Center (SELC) have noted how Elon Musk’s Colossus xAI data centers in Memphis disproportionately pollute the air in minority neighborhoods. A joint lawsuit by SELC, Earthjustice, and the NAACP filed last April argued that Musk and friends didn’t bother to get the necessary permits to run the 57 gas turbines powering the system.

The lawsuit points out that his Memphis-area data centers are violating the Clean Air Act, funneling all manner of pollutants into minority neighborhoods that already see a disproportionately high number of pollution-caused childhood illnesses:

“xAI’s power plant in Southaven has the potential to emit more than 1,700 tons of smog-forming nitrogen oxides (NOx) each year. The staggering emissions numbers likely make the facility the largest industrial source of NOx in the greater Memphis area, an area already failing to meet national smog standards. The illegal turbines also have the potential to release up to 180 tons of fine particulate matter, 500 tons of carbon monoxide, and 19 tons of formaldehyde—a toxic, cancer-causing chemical—each year.“

The Trump administration had tried to intervene on behalf of their favorite billionaire authoritarian, leveraging the power of the DOJ to claim that holding Musk accountable for violating environmental law would run in contrast to the country’s national security interests. The admin also ham-fistedly tried to have the Trump EPA take over the lawsuit as plaintiff and “voluntarily dismiss” the case.

Apparently advertising that fact wasn’t a particularly smart idea. US District Judge Debra Brown ‌last week issued a ruling stating the US Environmental Protection Agency could intervene in the case but lacks authority under the Clean Air Act to unilaterally terminate the lawsuit after joining it.

“The EPA’s role as a primary enforcer of the Clean Air Act does not mean that the federal government retains complete control over all Clean Air Act litigation,” Judge Brown wrote.

A cornerstone of the Trump administration has been a close collaboration with oligarchs and corporate power to hijack the courts, then obliterate already extremely shaky regulatory autonomy and corporate oversight. While the gambit has been broadly successful, likely culminating in decades of avoidable deaths and suffering, every so often the court system still procedurally balks at Trump’s ham-fisted corruption.

“The NAACP, along with our partners, is pleased that the Fifth Circuit Court recognized the importance of following Civil Procedure 101,” Abre’ Conner, NAACP Director of Environmental and Climate Justice, said of the ruling. “The DOJ tried an end run to the court of appeals, but its effort did not work in its favor. Our case has always been about holding polluters accountable and making sure that entities follow the law. The court made clear today that the law applies to everyone, including the federal government. We look forward to continuing our fight against pollution in the courtroom.”

items.title: Nvidia Chief Seen As Target of Chinese Spy Plot
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from The New York Times: American spy agencies had gathered striking intelligence. A top executive at a Singapore-based data center company was under scrutiny for possibly steering advanced Nvidia A.I. chips to China. And now American officials had concluded that she was a Chinese intelligence asset (source paywalled; alternative source), funneling information to Beijing. But what came next was even more alarming. Surveillance of the executive, Alice Huang or Huang Le, a Chinese citizen, revealed that she had developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang, Nvidia's chief executive.
 
For years, Washington has worked to deny China the technology needed to match or surpass the United States in the intense global competition for superiority in artificial intelligence. The discovery that Beijing was getting reports from someone with direct access to Mr. Huang, one of the most powerful figures in the A.I. revolution as well as an influential ally of President Trump's, set off alarms at the White House. Roughly a year ago, Mr. Trump was briefed about the intelligence findings, which have not been previously reported, and chose not to do anything with the information. Mr. Trump has been wary of disrupting Nvidia's chip sales, which are helping to drive the economy and the stock market, and of further complicating the trading relationship with China.
 
This account is based on interviews with people briefed on the surveillance, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because the findings are drawn from classified intelligence, as well as other officials and industry executives and analysts. American officials already suspected that Ms. Huang was helping China evade constraints on its ability to gain access to advanced A.I. chips. But the revelation that she was feeding information directly to Beijing raised more troubling possibilities, including that Mr. Huang had insights into Mr. Trump's thinking on an issue of vital importance to both nations, one likely to come up when the president visits China next month. And it left questions about whether she could be gleaning information about Nvidia, which as much as any company accounts for the lead the United States has maintained in developing cutting-edge A.I. models. The surveillance of Ms. Huang continues, they said, and companies that have been affiliated with her continued this year to purchase Nvidia chips. 

Nvidia said in a statement: "Jensen's interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO's job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year." Nvidia is "confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know." Customers like Megaspeed, the company that employed Ms. Huang, "receive ordinary business information -- not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets -- and zero information relevant to national security," the company added.
 
In a statement to The New York Times, Megaspeed said that its "current leadership" takes the matter "extremely seriously and is committed to getting to the facts behind these allegations." It added that "outside counsel has been retained to conduct a thorough internal investigation and has notified the U.S. government that we are fully committed to cooperating."

items.title: Massive Fanfic Site Archive of Our Own Says It’s Going Down for 'Up to 4 Weeks'
items.author: Samantha Cole
items.content:
Archive of Our Own (AO3), a massive repository for fanfiction and creative writing, might be down for as long as a month after going down for "maintenance" on Thursday.

The Organization for Transformative Works (OTW), the non-profit organization that runs AO3, posted on its status page early Thursday morning that the site was down for maintenance. A few hours later, it updated the status to say that it was expected to take at least 12 hours. By Thursday afternoon, it said the site restoration will take around two weeks, but could take up to a month.

“We are hopeful that we will be able to bring the site back up in a degraded state sooner. If that does happen, there may be times when the site has to be brought down temporarily until this is fully resolved. Please stay tuned for further info,” OTW wrote.

A spokesperson for OTW told 404 Media Thursday night that there are no more updates at this time beyond what's on the status page. They did, however, say that they don't expect there to be data loss. Early Friday morning, OTW added an update to the status page: "First, no AO3 data has been deleted. All your works, bookmarks, kudos, etc., are safe," it says. "Second, while we currently don't believe that the user database was stolen, we are also unable to rule it out. The AO3 database contains account information that may include your username, email address, IP address, and a hashed version of your password." They say they use hashing techniques to protect password data, but recommend users change their passwords on any other sites where they use the same password as on AO3, as a precaution.

It’s difficult to overstate the importance of AO3 to fan culture, fanfiction writers and readers, and its influence on internet culture in general. As of September, the open-source fanfic repository hosted over 18.4 million works spanning over 82,900 fandoms. This status update means AO3 is expected to be down during much of , most of new book release week, and on the cusp of the month formerly known as NaNoWriMo. If you were going as Ebony Dark'ness Dementia Raven Way for Halloween, you are in our thoughts. And if you have something to share about AO3’s extended shutdown and how it will affect the fanfic community, I'd love to hear from you: sam@404media.co.

Updated to add OTW comment and Friday morning's status page update.

items.title: The Streisand Effect Case Might Have Played Out Differently In Germany
items.author: Mike Masnick
items.content:
Streisand demanded $50 million in damages ($10 million for each of five counts). It quickly came out that prior to the lawsuit, the photo had been accessed a grand total of six times, and two of them were by Streisand’s lawyers. But after the lawsuit was filed, more than 420,000 people went to view the photo in the following month alone. California’s anti-SLAPP law protected Adelman, and Streisand was eventually forced to pay $177,107.54 in legal fees, including $155,567.04 to Adelman.

The story is remembered for the effect I coined, in part because of the futility of trying to hide information, but in part because it’s a reminder of the importance of free speech.

It’s possible that story would go very differently in Germany today. We already know that Germany is much more sensitive to concerns about privacy and data collection, and when Google launched its useful “Street View” feature in Google Maps, some people in Germany insisted it was a violation of their privacy. I have difficulty seeing how a single static photograph of buildings taken from public streets can be a privacy violation, but German regulators and plenty of residents insisted otherwise, so Google now lets residents blur out their own house in street view (and, tellingly, fewer than 3% of German households actually bothered to do so).

The German court ruled that Google acquired the aerial images by “spying” on ordinary people because it does not inform property owners beforehand that their homes will be filmed and photographed. As a result, Google does not get their consent to publish aerial photos and information about their property on its Maps and Earth sites.

The German court determined that Google had violated the privacy of the man and his family by sharing aerial images of their property on. It found that a person’s right to privacy extends across their entire property, not just inside their home.

“Nobody must accept the worldwide publication of aerial images of their property without their consent, at least when concerning areas of a property hidden from public view,” the court says in the ruling, according to DW.

The case concerned whether a property owner can demand that their inhabited property disappear from Google Earth and Google Maps or be blurred. The plaintiff lives with his family in a house in Frankfurt. At his request, his house had already been pixelated in Street View and Apple Look Around. However, in Google Earth and the 3D view of Google Maps, it remained visible as a three-dimensional model – including the rear portions of the property that are not visible from the street.

That same source notes that there is conflicting caselaw in Germany already though:

Neither ruling is precedential until there are higher court rulings.

The court also brushed aside Google’s argument that it was democratizing access to knowledge, admitting that was important, but saying that the privacy rights outweigh the access to information claims. Though the report notes Google may still appeal.

Maybe this is just cultural differences, but I find the whole thing bizarre. The court tries to limit this to parts of a property ‘hidden from public view,’ but that’s what an overhead photo is: a periodically updated snapshot of what anyone in a plane could see. Ongoing or real-time surveillance might be a different story. A static image from the sky is not that.

But, I guess Barbra should have moved to Frankfurt if she wanted to keep aerial photos of her home off the internet.

items.title: Canada to Join EU Network of Supercomputers
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Canada is joining the European Union's supercomputing network to give Canadian companies, startups, and researchers access to European computing resources for AI development. The partnership aims to strengthen AI cooperation and reduce dependence on US technology. Politico reports: The EU's supercomputing network is run by the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking, an EU public-private vehicle with an 8.2 billion-euro budget. The network consists of 14 supercomputers (some ranked in the global top 10), 19 AI-focused AI factories and 10 quantum computers. The vehicle will also run seven massive AI data center hubs, known as AI gigafactories, set to be built next year with a total investment cost of 30 billion euros.
 
Experts praised a possible EU-Canadian compute power team-up, but warned it's only the start. "Compute cooperation is one of the most obvious short-term 'middle power' cooperation plays in AI," said Anton Leicht, technology and international affairs fellow at Carnegie Endowment for International Peace. But he added that for now "it doesn't put a dent into the actual dependence" on the U.S. "As long as the U.S. builds gigawatt-scale clusters, no amount of cooperation that doesn't result in massive buildouts will help," he said.
 
Canada's engagement in the EU's supercomputer network builds further on Canada's previous partial involvement in the EU's flagship research and development program, Horizon Europe. Horizon Europe partially funds EuroHPC. To date, 38 countries have participated in the EU's supercomputing network: 27 EU member countries plus non-EU countries including Norway, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, Israel and Turkey.

items.title: Fifth Circuit Flips Earlier Ruling, Once Again Declares Migrants Have No Due Process Rights
items.author: Tim Cushing
items.content:
The Fifth Circuit has shown itself to be especially subservient to the Trump administration since his return to office. And it’s certainly not going to rock Trump’s mass deportation boat — not when it’s sitting right on top of Texas, which contains almost two-thirds of the US-Mexico border, as well as some of ICE’s largest detention facilities.

It’s been several months of back-and-forth at the Fifth. While it has long been held that migrants living in the US are afforded the same rights as US citizens, the Fifth Circuit has done its best to ignore this. In February of this year, it simply decided — in opposition to hundreds of federal rulings across the nation — that detained migrants could be subjected to indefinite detainment without a bond hearing.

It chose to believe what the DOJ told it to believe: that there was no difference between someone detained illegally crossing a border and someone swept up by ICE’s kidnapping squads after living peacefully and productively in the US for months, if not years or decades.

Then in July it pulled back a bit from that precipice. While it couldn’t be convinced to fully support rights recognized everywhere else in the Fifth Circuit, it did at least put a time limit on constitutional rights violations. While most courts have reasonably found that any rights violation begins the moment the right is violated, the Fifth Circuit declared the government could ignore migrants’ due process rights immediately… but only for 90 days.

Apparently, that wasn’t acceptable for the more far-right cheerleaders on the Fifth Circuit’s bench. Less than a week later, the Fifth Circuit announced it would be rehearing this case in front of the whole roster of judges — the sort of thing a court only says when most of those judges disagree with respecting long-held rights.

Sure enough, that’s exactly what happened. The hearing has rolled back the already-wrong “rights, but only after 90 days” decision handed down during the first week of July. We’re back to where we were in February: no due process rights for migrants, no matter how long they’ve been detained or how long they’d already resided in this country when they were arrested. (h/t Chris Geidner)

The new decision [PDF] simply says migrants don’t have any rights, even though this puts the Fifth Circuit in opposition of hundreds of federal courts and tens of thousands of court rulings:

We now conclude that Petitioners were not entitled to individual hearings on their dangerousness or flight risk before they could be lawfully detained by immigration authorities pending their removal proceedings. Moreover, the duration of Petitioners’ detention presented no constitutional issues warranting habeas relief.

And while thousands of decisions have made it clear the law this administration has chosen to abuse via an extremely novel interpretation of the phrase “applicants for admission” (something that has historically been applied exclusive to people confronted by immigration agents when attempting to cross the border) doesn’t actually say what the government wants it to say (that any migrant in the country for whatever length of time is no different than someone apprehended during the act of crossing the border), the Fifth Circuit goes the other way.

Then it shrugs and says that if plaintiffs want this fixed, they should talk to Congress. But Congress has already made it clear that due process rights apply to residing in this county and that the exception applies to people apprehended while crossing the border. This is the court giving Trump what wants while pretending is to blame for this sudden, one-circuit-only refusal to recognize migrants’ due process rights.

Controlling illegal immigration is, no doubt, an important and controversial issue of public policy. But the Constitution entrusts broad authority to delineate immigration policy, and to design proceedings to effectuate those policy choices, to Congress—not courts.

Bullshit. This ruling is nothing more than cowardice from a majority of Fifth Circuit judges who don’t want to cross Trump and are more than willing to blame their own lack of spine on the legislative branch. Also included are 70 pages of concurrences and dissenting opinions. The dissents point out the obvious: the Fifth Circuit is interpreting the law in a way Congress never intended, or even merely hinted at over the past few decades. The concurrences just want to see the rights removed. The worst of those is Judge James Ho, who claims the dissenters are more interested in protecting the rights of migrants than US citizens:

Alas, such passion for liberty has been lacking have been detained for expressing opinions disfavored by government officials. See, e.g., Villarreal v. City of Laredo, 134 F.4th 273 (5th Cir. 2025), reaff’g 94 F.4th 374 (5th Cir. 2024); Gonzalez v. Trevino, 60 F.4th 906 (5th Cir. 2023); see also Mayfield v. Butler Snow, L.L.P., 78 F.4th 796 (5th Cir. 2023).

My point is not to relitigate those cases, but to contrast the dissent’s votes in those cases with its views today. It’s to point out that liberty wasn’t favored for citizens who seek to vindicate their constitutional rights—but it’s cherished for illegal aliens who seek to violate our national sovereignty.

Only of the dissenters in this case (Stewart) agreed with the ruling in — a case in which the majority blessed vindictive prosecution of a police critic. of the dissenters in this due process case were part of the majority decision that said — again — that it’s okay to engage in vindictive prosecution of a government critic (). And James Ho himself heard the final case he cites (), delivering the blow to constitutional rights himself, which makes it extremely disingenuous for him to call out these judges (who weren’t actually part of the hearing panels) for expressing their dissent at that point in time.

The end result is the same as it was back in July. Texas will be the destination of choice for the Trump administration, which now knows for certain it won’t be forced to respect due process rights. And the Fifth will get back to its day-to-day business of being the worst circuit in the nation — a place where constitutional rights (except the 2nd Amendment!) go to die.

items.title: 'Please Let the Internet Die'
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Slashdot reader fjo3 shares an article from Wired: The internet must be put out of its misery. Any rational observer can admit that the current iteration of the web -- and the social fabric woven there -- is not what they signed up for. Symptoms of advanced cultural decay can no longer be ignored. This thing is eating itself. Giants including Meta and Google have been forced to settle massive consumer lawsuits brought over privacy violations and mental health harms allegedly caused by the addictive mechanisms of their platforms. Schools are banning smartphones as multiple countries institute social media restrictions for under-16s. Parents are in a panic about their kids aspiring to careers as social media celebrities, losing themselves in a vast ecosystem of online casinos, or joining extremist movements. Generative AI, briefly considered an amusing novelty, is now a turbocharged slop engine for the web, filling feeds and comment sections with useless, grotesque content. As humans scroll past headlines about AI taking their jobs, confusing fantasy for reality, and contributing to cognitive decline, any consumer appeal the technology might have is turning to anguish. The data centers that power it have become increasingly unpopular, and politically radioactive.
 
To be online, many now admit, is to be endlessly manipulated and exploited. In December, Oxford University Press declared rage bait to be the word of the year, noting that use of the term had tripled over the previous 12 months. The lexical spike represented a heightened awareness that monetized social accounts churn out bad-faith takes and extremist content, automating this abusive behavior with generative AI, simply to profit off hostile engagement. Billionaire oligarchs have opened the floodgates to such inauthentic activity, conspiracy-mongering, and hate speech by rolling back moderation. In short, when you hang around online in 2026, you see little worth saving. Perhaps a decade ago, you felt that the glimmers of community and joy, of artistic and intellectual exchange, were enough to balance out the toxic junk. No longer.

items.title: Manifestos, Fear, and ‘Loser Thinking’: Inside Proton’s AI Reckoning
items.author: Joseph Cox
items.content:
Andy Yen, the CEO of Proton, had a message for an employee in the company’s security Slack channel who urged the company to at least take a few days to pentest newly written code before pushing it live. “That’s bullshit and loser thinking. Of course it’s possible to be fast and secure,” Yen wrote in the channel at the end of August. “Stop thinking always of how to be slower, and focus more on how to be faster.”

In a follow-up message, Yen reiterated his point: “only losers think like that.” His ultimate message for the team was to “stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more.”

That exchange was just one of many that showed how Yen and other company executives are aggressively pushing Proton towards AI. Proton is a Swiss company that famously makes the encrypted email service Proton Mail and a suite of privacy and security-focused products, including an encrypted drive service, an authenticator app, a password manager, and more.

In the last few months, Yen set up an email address for employees to contact if they come across anything blocking adoption of AI at Proton, so leadership can “ruthlessly smash everything that stands in the way of AI velocity;” Proton installed software on workers’ computers that track how much AI code the company is generating; and Yen said this is the last year that Proton will hire engineers at all, and instead only hire people to build things with AI.

That AI push came to head this week when Proton said it would re-interview staff about their use of AI, with the clear implication that those interviews, and employees’ willingness to embrace AI, could decide whether a worker is fired or not.

404 Media spoke to eight current and one former Proton employees and reviewed Slack chats, meeting recordings, and an AI manifesto written by the company’s CTO. Our reporting reveals a culture of fear inside Proton, where many employees are hesitant to even mildly critique Yen’s views or discuss engineering problems. Workers describe an environment where employees have genuine concerns about security or being asked to develop security products with AI, but feel unable to voice them, lest Yen berates them in front of everyone or threatens their employment at the company.

“The CEO is in full AI psychosis and has been for a while now,” one of the sources told 404 Media.

Our reporting also paints a picture of Proton that is likely very different to the public’s perception of a company with a goal of carefully protecting privacy: one that in reality is barreling ahead with AI as quickly as possible so it can achieve the explicit goal of more annual revenue.

“Due to insufficient velocity,” Proton is not on track to achieve its annual recurring revenue target by the end of the year, one internal document obtained by 404 Media reads. Proton’s year-over-year growth is also “far away from what the market today considers to be good,” and, “By all metrics that matter, we’re an underperforming company.”

In response to detailed questions from 404 Media, a Proton spokesperson did not dispute any of our reporting or characterization of what’s happening inside of the company. 

“It’s clear that some people at Proton are unhappy with our direction, or misunderstand it, and many people are anxious,” they said. “In our determination to move fast, we have sometimes been too blunt or too slow in explaining ourselves to our people. We will work on that, as their questions are the ones we most need to answer.”

Do you know anything else about Proton? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at joseph.404 or send me an email at joseph@404media.co.

Yen, a former CERN particle physicist, projects a measured approach in public, but internally he acts more like what one employee described as a “petulant child.” In May, Proton announced it was implementing post-quantum cryptography which should protect against future attacks from quantum computers. The work took years of effort, with one caveat that it would not work on older emails, only those written after the feature’s launch, at least for the moment. Yen was not happy that Proton was drawing attention to this limitation.

I recently noted how California’s being told by the Trump administration that it can’t enforce any of its own telecom consumer protection laws if it wants to receive $1.4 billion dollars Congress already earmarked for broadband expansion under the 2021 infrastructure bill.

That means if California wants money it was already supposed to receive from Congress, it can’t enforce its own net neutrality law, telecom privacy law, affordability metrics, reliability targets, or effectively do anything telecom monopoly giants like AT&T and Comcast don’t like.

More specifically, some extremely unpopular Trump NTIA revisions to the infrastructure bill’s Broadband, Equity, Access, and Deployment (BEAD) program included a little something called “Condition 50,” which would impose a 14 year moratorium on telecom consumer protection in the state. It’s just grotesque levels of corruption and regulatory capture, and it’s flown largely under the radar.

Tim Wu (Columbia), Lawrence Lessig and Yochai Benkler (Harvard), Jack Balkin (Yale), Zephyr Teachout (Fordham), and Barbara van Schewick (Stanford) have penned a joint letter to Gavin Newsom urging him to refuse to sign the state’s BEAD notice of award agreement while Condition 50 is still attached. Or, better yet, legally challenge the federal government extortion:

“California must decide by November 1 whether to sign the Notice of Award for its $1.42 billion BEAD grant. We urge the State not to sign while Condition 50 remains attached, with or without a side letter. The best course is to challenge Condition 50 in court before the deadline: California has strong arguments that NTIA lacked authority to impose the condition, but it has a realistic chance of winning only if it sues before signing the award. If the State decides not to sue, it should decline the award and make clear that California is ready to accept the funds as soon as the condition is removed.”

(Since the letter’s writing the deadline has shifted to November 2, I’m told). If California signs the letter with Condition 50 attached, the Trump NTIA will argue the challenge belongs in D.C. federal court under a very narrow standard of review, and that California knowingly accepted the condition. Such a case would be extremely difficult to win, the academics note.

Given the total collapse of federal consumer protection and regulatory integrity, AT&T, Comcast, and other giants would be free to rip off consumers — and undermine competitors — with impunity.

Public Knowledge, EFF, Free Press, Demand Progress, Fight for the Future, TURN, groups representing rural and low-income Californians, leaders of the Lower Russian River Firewise Communities, the Communications Workers of America, and the California Democratic Party’s Rural Caucus have also joined the calls to fight back against the Trump administration before the November 2 deadline.

It’s worth noting that every other state has signed their letter to receive their funds, in part because telecom lobbying has already neutered state autonomy over broadband in those states. Thirty-three states and D.C. bar their utility commissions from regulating broadband, and in seven more the commission has disclaimed that authority “on its own” (read: AT&T told them to).

The efforts to muzzle California’s consumer protection capabilities is just one of numerous extremely unpopular and corrupt changes made to the infrastructure bill program to the benefit of either massive monopolies — or Elon Musk.

I’ve explored at length (at several different outlets) how $42.5 billion in BEAD funding was supposed to be headed to the states to address broadband improvements. Instead, the Trump administration has hijacked the program, driven billions of dollars of those funds to Musk for inferior satellite service (he’d already planned to deploy without subsidy), and stripped the program of any requirement that these taxpayer funds be dispersed equitably or with an eye on affordability.

You know, because cheap, ultra-fast, fiber optic cable that challenges Comcast is .

The $42.5 billion in BEAD money states were supposed to get for broadband upgrades was already effectively cut in half after the Trump administration engaged in Elon Musk favoritism. That meant a lot of money previously slated for cheap, future-proof fiber will instead be redirected to Musk’s increasingly congested Starlink Low-Earth-Orbit satellite network.

Now states are being told they won’t get if they engage in policy choices big telecom giants don’t like, including enforcing basic reliability and affordability protections.

items.title: Google Struggling to Make AI Mode Searches Pay
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Alphabet shares fell nearly 10% after Google disclosed that searches through its AI Mode generate less revenue than traditional search, even as overall search revenue grew 12% year over year to $63.25 billion. The Register reports: Alphabet on Wednesday reported its Q3 results, which included news that its year-over-year search query growth rate is the highest it's been in the last five years. Some of that growth comes from users adopting "AI Mode" -- Google's latest LLM-powered search system. Google's revenue from search rose 12 percent year-over-year to $63.25 billion, a little lower than the 14.5 percent growth the company reported in last year's Q3.
 
During Alphabet's earnings call, chief business officer Philipp Schindler said the slowdown was caused by "lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode." That's a worry given that Google is spending enormous sums on infrastructure. $51.4 billion went out the door in Q3, around two thirds of it going towards servers and networking equipment. The rest funded datacenter builds. That spending appears to have impacted profitability, as Alphabet reported $26.17 billion net income for the quarter. Last year's Q3, during which Google revenue was $102.35 billion, produced $35 billion net income.
 
Schindler argued that AI search will pay off. "On AI Mode, many of these queries are upper funnel queries, allowing us to capture new, high-value commercial intent," he told investors. "In addition, the majority of AI Mode queries are incremental, creating more monetization opportunities over time." Google tried to seize one of those opportunities today, by turning on ads alongside AI Mode searches around the world, after first testing them in the US only. But for now, AI Mode searches aren't as lucrative as Google's existing search business, which brought in just under half of Alphabet's $125.8 billion quarterly revenue.

items.title: Senators Demand Meta Answer for 'Pervert Glasses' Following 404 Media Investigation
items.author: Samantha Cole
items.content:
Oregon Senator Ron Wyden and Massachusetts Senator Edward Markey sent a letter to Meta on Wednesday demanding the company answer for the privacy concerns its smart glasses pose to the public. 

The letter cites 404 Media’s October 2025 investigation into how people use Meta’s smart glasses to harass massage parlor workers. That investigation found Instagram accounts with hundreds of thousands of followers and millions of views uploaded videos filmed with Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses, where men entered massage parlors across the country and solicited the workers for sex work. The

“Meta’s own disclosures confirm that imagery processed through its glasses’ visual AI features may be retained and used to train AI systems, including with the assistance of human reviewers,” the letter says. “Using intimate imagery for AI development is itself an invasion of privacy when the people depicted have not consented to that use, as is inherently the case for most bystanders captured by Meta’s glasses. Retaining that material for AI development, thereby extending the period during which it can be accessed, disclosed, or misused, exploits people’s highly sensitive information for Meta’s commercial benefit.”

Research revealed how Meta’s platforms encourage an ecosystem of abusive, harassing content from pickup artists and influencers who use Meta’s smart glasses to capture interactions with people minding their own business in public or at their workplaces, who might not even know they’re being filmed. In a January report by the BBC, a woman who was recorded with the glasses said she was “bombarded” with phone calls because her phone number was posted with the video, and men who had seen the video stalked her at work.

, more than 70 people sued Meta, claiming that their intimate images and videos were exposed to workers hired by the company to label the data for AI. In March, Swedish journalists reported that Kenyan data labelers were viewing and annotating uncensored footage from Meta’s smart glasses, including sexual and violent content; Meta ended its contract with those workers less than two months later. These are labor conditions that groups like the Data Labelers Association in Kenya are , and for the people whose images are in the videos and photos, it’s an obvious violation of their privacy. People have also been to disable the light that indicates they’re recording for years 

Meta has about the difference between AI glasses you wear on your face and an iPhone for a long time. Now, these senators want the tech giant to answer for themselves. In the letter, Wyden and Markey demand answers about what safeguards, if any, Meta has in place to prevent the nonconsensual “capture, disclosure, or processing of sensitive and intimate imagery,” whether Meta specifically evaluated the potential for its glasses “to facilitate voyeurism, nonconsensual intimate image capture, or similar privacy invasions,” what imagery it uses for AI training, and whether people can request their biometric and other data captured by its glasses be deleted, along with several more questions about the glasses’ safety and design.

“The reported disclosure of intimate footage to contractors for the purpose of AI training is particularly disturbing. Human review to fulfill a service knowingly requested by the person depicted is one thing; exposing unsuspecting individuals’ intimate moments to strangers for AI training is quite another,” Wyden and Markey wrote. “The individuals whose naked bodies, sexual activity, and other private moments have reportedly been captured by Meta glasses did not knowingly agree to having those images shared with strangers, much less for the purpose of improving Meta’s commercial AI systems. That disclosure and processing is an invasion of privacy, regardless of whether the footage is subsequently published or misused.” 

Do you know anything else about harassment and Meta's smart glasses? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at sam.404. Otherwise, send me an email at sam@404media.co.

In the last few weeks, for quietly changing its privacy policies for business accounts and granting itself permission to scrape user’s content and connected websites to develop its AI products. 

Meta has been pushing its smart glasses over the years with ads featuring A-list celebrities, including Chris Pratt, Chris Hemsworth, and Kris Jenner (all three in ), from K-pop group BLACKPINK, and most recently, . Guerrilla ad makers have countered with their own ads around the world, and people have started calling the smart glasses "pervert glasses" in response to these widespread invasions of privacy they've come to represent. In August, Meta to add facial recognition and highlight reel features to its smart glasses.

items.title: Ink Droplets In Motion Snag Top Prize In Nikon Small World Contest
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
A 25-year-old German photographer won the 2026 Nikon Small World competition with a microscopic image freezing ink droplets in midair as an inkjet printer deposits them onto paper. Ars Technica reports that Ole Bielfeldt "beat out 1,802 other entries hailing from 69 different countries." From the report: Bielfeldt became interested in photomicrography during the COVID-19 lockdown after discovering an old microscope in his parents' attic. He figured out how to build an adaptor out of a tube and some wood to connect the microscope to his father's camera and taught himself the art through trial and error, building custom tools as needed. He documents how he captures transformative images of everyday objects with behind-the-scenes videos posted to macrofying, his photography and videography brand.
 
It was Bielfeldt's curiosity about the inner workings of inkjet printers that inspired his winning entry, but capturing the action of ink drops being deposited on paper was a challenge, given that the process happens so quickly. The droplets, for instance, moved faster than the camera's shutter speed. Bielfeldt's solution was to deconstruct the printer so that the paper moved under a stationary (rather than moving) printhead, and then take the image in a dark room, using a flash to serve as the shutter, thereby freezing the ink drops mid-air. There was no need for pricey equipment. Bielfeldt does not use AI in his images, preferring to rely on traditional techniques. "Ole Bielfeldt's winning image embodies what makes Nikon Small World so powerful: the intersection of microscope imaging, ingenuity, and artistry," said Eric Flem, a spokesperson for Nikon Instruments. "By using a microscope objective in a different way, he transformed a familiar object into something altogether new and previously unseen. It is a reminder that the microscope is not only a scientific tool but also a creative one, capable of expanding how we see and imagine the world around us."
 
The full list of winners can be found here.

items.title: Tim Sweeney Would Be Well Served To Stop Talking About AI Right About Now
items.author: Timothy Geigner
items.content:
It’s probably a good thing for Tim Sweeney that Epic Games is a privately held company and he has a majority ownership stake, because I can’t imagine any Board of Directors would appreciate this AI rager he’s been on as of late. And, somehow, it keeps getting worse. It all started with Sweeney absurdly claiming that Steam, Epic’s chief rival, requiring AI use disclosures on game pages was somehow “irresponsible.” In an arena in which many among gaming consumers care very much about whether games use generative AI or not, advocating for those same consumers to be willfully less informed is quite the choice. Then Epic leadership dictated to its staff that heavy use of AI in games was compulsory, rather than just another tool to be used by artists. And then Epic hit the AI idiocy trifecta by bragging about a new vibe-coded game launcher that largely sucked and, for the areas the company claimed had largely been improved, those gains were outpaced by Steam one short update later.

On Friday, AI bro Matt Workman posted to his X account that “the premise of an AI Generated Content Disclosure is ABSURD in 2026,” calling it “truly embarrassing for a Valve and Steam.” Sweeney enthusiastically replied.

If you can’t see that, it’s Sweeney saying:

Forcing developers to write a political statement to be used against them by the hate mob they’re helping organize is abhorrent.

A political statement? ? Under no reasonable definition is the disclosure of the use of AI — a factual statement — a political statement. The disclosures say nothing about what be, only what .

I have very little respect for Kotaku when it comes to its content concerning the use of AI in gaming, but on this particular matter, its analysis is spot on. Sweeney is attempting to rope politics in where it doesn’t belong to hand-wave away the dissent from the very gaming public he seeks to make more ignorant about what they’re buying.

Calling things a “political statement” is a fun game played by those who like to suggest that anything with which they disagree must by necessity be some wack-a-doo extreme political position. Presumably Sweeney also considers the listing of ingredients on a food wrapper to be a “political statement,” forced by the wokies who demand consumers know if their dinner contains anthrax or worms.

Sweeney is suggesting that the required AI disclosures are causing “hate mobs” to go after developers who post them, adding later that “there is a real economic cost to Valve’s foray into forced political disclosures. Beside taking 30%, they’re also taking a potentially even larger fraction of developers’ revenues and livelihood by undermining their businesses with these AI hate campaigns.” For important context, Steam’s AI declarations are buried at the bottom of a store page in small text, alongside any content warnings. The word “potentially” is doing an awful lot of work in that statement.

There is a way Sweeney could have been an AI advocate for gaming, even if you think the technology has no place in the industry. There are grounds for a conversation here. But just like the never-AI crowd takes themselves out of that conversation by the very nature of their stance, so too do clowns like Sweeney remove themselves from the conversation when they are so absurdly planted on the other end of the spectrum. The moment you’re suggesting that customer concerns and desires should be addressed by non-disclosure of the facts they care about, and then further likening them to a mob because they don’t agree with you, you’ve lost the plot. And lost it badly.

That’s Sweeney brushing away someone pointing out that Epic’s own Fab marketplace requires AI disclosure, saying:

This is a business to business marketplace. Many Fab customers are operating under contracts that require them to understand the providence [sic] of all content in their game (including Steam’s own contract that I’ve complained about) and they cannot buy assets without this info.

The point isn’t that Sweeney is wrong about those nuanced circumstances. The point is that lots of people can make arguments of that sort, including Steam, which is offered no quarter by Sweeney.

Again, there are right ways to have this conversation. Sweeney’s antics ain’t it. Instead, he’s become perhaps the number one avatar for all the things the anti-AI crowd says they’re worried about. And when it comes to Sweeney and Epic, it’s hard to argue with them.

items.title: Anthropic Engineer Declares the Coding Interview Dead
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
An Anthropic engineering manager says he has stopped using traditional coding interviews because AI can now outperform candidates on the kinds of programming challenges they typically contain. "There's no more point in giving you a little React challenge than there is in quizzing people about assembly; Claude is now better at both," said Felix Rieseberg in a blog post. "Our most impactful builders are successful regardless of how good they are at these tests." The Register reports: "I don't think the coding interview is going to come back," said Rieseberg. "It's easy to get sentimental given how many copies of 'Algorithms and Data Structures' were bought in hopes of unlocking good jobs and a better future -- or how the death of the coding interview is another milestone in software engineering reaching a new level of abstraction."
 
At the same time, he's not certain what will replace it. "I'm probably not the only manager trying to figure out how to interview for people who build well with AI," Rieseberg wrote. "I haven't quite gotten there yet -- but I'm scanning resumes and portfolios for little prototypes that exhibit taste, empathy, and principled thinking. If you have figured out something better, I'd love to hear how." 
In a response posted to social media, Jaana Dogan, principal engineer at Google, said: "I'm not doing a ton of coding interviews nowadays but I'd be interested to interview how people use coding agents," she wrote. "That itself gives me more signals about candidates' coding skills."
 
"We are not seeing tech companies abandon skills assessments widely across the industry -- at least not yet," added Nicole Bachaud, labor economist at ZipRecruiter. "In fact, based on our October 2026 Employer Survey of 1,500 employers, we see the tech industry (Information sector specifically) is actually the most likely to test for skills, with 62.5 percent of employers requiring formal skill tests on initial applications."
 
"The change at Anthropic might be reflecting a shift away from technical skills towards more human, soft skills," said Bachaud. "As AI becomes fully capable of writing code, tech employers may be pivoting away from rote technical testing and heavily toward human-centric soft skills." She argues that while AI may be able to code well, it can't replace critical thinking. "A staggering 61.5 percent of Information employers now report that 'critical thinking' is a primary skill lacking in today's candidate pool," she said.

items.title: The Metric Is Not The Mission: The Full Paper
