Over the last few months, we’ve been running the wonderful ten part series on “The Metric is Not the Mission” by Konstantinos Komaitis. It’s a deep exploration of how Big Tech moved from building and expanding the open internet to increasingly shaping it around its own metrics, incentives and assumptions. The resulting series explores how things went from building a better, more open, more beneficial internet… to whatever it is that we have now.

In the latter half, it also explores what happens next, the reckoning that the big companies face from regulators and litigation, and points towards a way to think through what comes next: hopefully bringing back a better internet for all of us.

From the beginning, we said that once the series was published, we’d publish a combined version in PDF form, and that’s what we have here: The Metric is not the Mission, in full as a single PDF file (also embedded at the end of this post).

If you didn’t read it while it was coming out in serialized fashion, you can now read the whole thing in one sitting. Or if you did read it, but want to read the whole thing again. Or even better, if you think there are other people who should read it, feel free to send it to them.

We’ve heard tremendous feedback from people who really enjoyed the series, and said it made them think. Thanks to Konstantinos for writing it and agreeing to have it published here.

items.title: Massive Leak Exposes 41,000 Homeland Security Workers
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
A massive leak has exposed records tied to more than 41,000 DHS employees and contractors, including roughly 10,000 ICE personnel. The data, reportedly taken from DHS's Okta login system, reveals phone numbers, email and office addresses, reporting relationships, and permission groups associated with undercover operations, wiretapping and surveillance tools. Wired reports: In all, the leak provides a map of how DHS is organized and how it operates. The records, which span DHS itself as well as seven component agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement and US Customs and Border Protection, were last updated on August 19, 2026.
 
The transparency nonprofit Distributed Denial of Secrets and cybersecurity researcher and journalist maia arson crimew previewed the data to WIRED, which they say they obtained from a group calling itself the Department of Peace. DDoSecrets published the archive, which it calls "Icepick," on Wednesday. In a press release, DDoSecrets says the data is from DHS's Okta login system. In a note with the files, the hackers wrote, "They have our information, so it's only fair that we have theirs." An Okta spokesperson tells WIRED that it is unaware of any breach of its systems. "We are aware of this report. Okta is secure, and we have no evidence our data or systems were compromised," the spokesperson says.

items.title: Latest Drop By Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoS) Contains Contact Info For 40,000 DHS Employees
items.author: Tim Cushing
items.content:
Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoS) has been steadily pushing the limits of transparency and accountability for several years now. The project — spearheaded by Emma Best — does what other activists won’t… or perhaps simply don’t have the expertise to carry out.

DDoS made a name for itself by hitching Best’s non-stop FOIA onslaught to data and info exfiltrated from government agencies by hackers and data breaches. Add it all together and it’s a project that actually delivers transparency and, consequently, increases government accountability.

From releasing files about Russia that Wikileaks selectively chose to ignore to dumping multiple terabytes of law enforcement helicopter camera footage none of these agencies would ever have voluntarily released, DDoS does what it says on the tin: refuses to let the government’s secrets remain secret.

Today, it’s releasing information on nearly 40,000 DHS employees — something that is estimated to cover nearly 20 percent of its total workforce. This covers all DHS component agencies, including ICE, CBP, HSI, and another dozen or so subsidiaries that don’t make the headlines nearly as often as the Big Three.

But it’s not just a data dump. As Best points out in DDoS’s press release, this info — leaked by an “Okta single sign-on service” — has not only been vetted, it’s been cleaned up to give viewers a clearer picture of organizational structures as well as make it easily searchable. It’s not about dumping data on thousands of foot soldiers. It’s about drawing connections between the boots on the ground and those who have put those boots on the ground.

”Rather than an indiscriminate directory of every DHS employee, Icepick identifies many of the architects and drivers of DHS policy and operations,” said journalist and DDoSecrets cofounder Emma Best. ”The leak is extraordinary but deceptive in it’s simplicity as it identifies the officials responsible for overseeing covert and undercover operations, the government’s hunt for leakers and the failed BlueLeaks investigation — along with key personnel in DHS’s ever-escalating rendition and deportation programs.”

The “Icepick” referred to by Best is the front-end for searching this database. The data on these 40,000 federal employees was obtained by a source that has only referred to itself as the “Department of Peace.” Journalist/hacktivist “crimew” (assisted by journalist Ryan Fae) did the dirty work of creating a rather sleek front end for the search engine, as well as doing the even dirtier work of cleaning up the data to deliver relevant results more frequently.

The end result is useful for everyone from journalists to people suing DHS employees. Here’s a sample shot providing details on David Easterwood, an ICE Deputy Field Office Director currently working in Minnesota:

Everything underlined is a link that opens a new search. It allows users to climb up the chain of command (the “Manager” field), as well as drill down to the specifics of those in Easterwood’s command (“Manager of”). It also pulls up a list of all related groups Easterwood is a member of in this Okta instance, ranging from the instantly worrying (ERO St Paul Intelligence Team) to the “it’s just offices all the way down” banality of “Adobe-Acrobat Pro DC Users.”

While it may have been possible to brute force email addresses by dialing in on shared nomenclature among federal agencies, it’s highly unlikely most people would be able to suss out direct phone lines, much less cell phone numbers. To be sure, this small amount of immediately visible (and searchable) info will provoke outlandish reactions from government officials. On the other hand, any arguments that this makes things more “dangerous” for DHS agents and officials should be immediately dismissed.

What this do is allow people to figure out who’s calling the shots wherever they’re experiencing surges in ICE activity and the violence that so often comes with it. And this allows plaintiffs seeking to hold the government accountable the ability to go up and down the chain of command to find names to add to lawsuits. If their rights were violated by masked ICE thugs in a certain area, perusing city and state data could potentially allow them to identify the officers who were directly responsible for these acts.

And, going back to the inevitable claims that this will allow people to “target” government agents, let’s not forget these same people have access to data about citizens and aren’t particularly shy about using that info to track and surveil critics and activists. The info released here shouldn’t make anyone fear for their safety. What it might do, however, is remind federal officers that they’re not untouchable.

Some onlookers, like progressive activist Leah Greenberg, marveled that "the fact that Marissa Mayer would voluntarily disclose this to a reporter is a pretty good demonstration of how deeply the culture of Silicon Valley has diverged from the rest of humanity." [...] After publication, Mayer defended herself in a long X post. She claims she was not relying on Dazzle to explain her child to her, but rather, she was testing what her prototype could do -- it resurfaced photos of "forgotten kindergarten projects," like a "snake devenomer" or "sandcat playground," illustrating her daughter's creativity and care for animals.
 
Fair enough. But Mayer remarks in the same interview that people could also use her AI to outsource the mental load of "figuring out the theme for your child's birthday party." She says she's used her app to plan a playdate for her daughter, book family activities on vacation, and decide what to be for Halloween. She even proposes that her AI assistant could coordinate plans with her husband's AI assistant. When the reporter asks her if it's depressing to imagine this "frictionless future planned by AI," Mayer replies, "I haven't really thought that through." The bigger question is: What should we outsource to AI? "What feels like grunt work to someone might be a meaningful part of parenthood for someone else," says Fortune's Emma Hinchliffe.
 
Michael Tasner, Founder and CEO of No Joke Marketing, adds: "Customers are drowning in AI slop, and they can spot it. Use AI for the low-stakes work behind the scenes. Keep the moments that matter to your customers human. Human connection is becoming the new premium."

items.title: Court Should Curb Abuse of Grand Jury Subpoenas Targeting Social Media Users
items.author: Mario Trujillo
items.content:
A federal appeals court should curb the government’s abuse of grand jury subpoenas to unmask social media users who criticize lawless immigration enforcement.

That is the message from the ACLU, EFF, and other civil liberties and trade groups who filed a friend-of-the-court brief in a sealed case in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia.

The case involves the government’s investigation of an anonymous Reddit user who commented on a post about an immigration officer in Minnesota. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) first issued an administrative subpoena to Reddit to unmask the user. When the user challenged the subpoena in court on free speech and statutory grounds (as many others have), DHS withdrew it. But then the government obtained a separate grand jury subpoena—a subpoena issued by a prosecutor to gather evidence to present to a grand jury before any criminal charges are filed—for much of the same information. The user then challenged the grand jury subpoena too, and the case is currently being appealed.

The right to speak anonymously is essential. It preserves privacy and shields critics from government retaliation. In the past year, the Department of Justice (DOJ) has issued grand jury subpoenas to social media companies for their users’ personal data. This is frequently done for improper purposes and without really showing that social media users have committed any crime. These subpoenas have the effect of intimidating and chilling critics, as immigration authorities have engaged in invasive, unconstitutional, and sometimes violent conduct.

As the amicus brief makes clear, courts should not defer to the government’s claims regarding the legitimacy of using grand jury subpoenas to unmask internet users. Instead, the subpoenas must receive proper First Amendment scrutiny. Like many other types of legal processes, grand jury subpoenas are issued by federal officials without prior court approval. And they too can be abused to harass or retaliate against people critical of the government.

The amicus brief was filed in early September and recently unsealed. The brief was signed by the American Civil Liberties Union of DC, EFF, the Center for Individual Rights, the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, the Cato Institute, and NetChoice.

It is notable that NetChoice signed the amicus brief. It is a trade group that represents many companies who have received similar subpoenas including Reddit, Google, Meta, PayPal, among others. EFF has called on these companies to do more to defend their users’ speech and privacy rights in the face of these subpoenas.

items.title: Amazon Finds 'Tokenmaxxing' Lacks Productivity Gains
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
Ancient Slashdot reader Gilmoure shares a report from Tom's Hardware, adding: "Huh. Looks like consuming one's own slop does not turn the wheels of industry." From the report: Amazon wants its engineers to quit chasing token counts, warning that heavy AI usage does not automatically mean better work. In updated engineering guidelines published on October 27, the company laid out how developers and managers should gauge AI's real impact -- and the takeaway is blunt: consuming more tokens is not the same as delivering more value. [...]
 
According to the memo, metrics such as AI adoption rates, token consumption, code changes, and code reviews become "deeply flawed" when they are disconnected from actual results. Turning them into targets, Amazon says, encourages wasteful behavior that clashes with its emphasis on "frugality and simplicity" and can raise both compute bills and software complexity.
 
The company's preferred yardstick is long-term results. "We believe that it is best to measure, and be measured by, long-term outcomes," Amazon wrote. That does not mean managers should ignore usage data altogether, as input metrics remain useful when examined "with care and judgment" alongside other indicators. Amazon suggests looking at both the teams using AI the least and those using it the most to determine whether adoption is translating into better delivery.
 
[...] The memo also pushes back on the idea that every task needs an AI tool. If current tooling does not benefit someone's work, Amazon says, that is "a finding, not a failing." Engineers who can explain where today's tools fall short are demonstrating judgment rather than reluctance to adopt AI.

items.title: Never Mind The Deepfakes, Chatbots Have To Deal With Election Lies Being Free, While Truth Is Paywalled
items.author: Mike Masnick
items.content:
It seems that every election cycle over the last decade has had concerns being raised about the state of “political deepfakes” and their ability to impact the election. So far, these have always been overblown, and there’s been little evidence of deepfakes having any real impact at all — perhaps other than creating the concept of “the liar’s dividend” enabling politicians caught doing actually bad things to falsely claim that it’s “fake news” and a “deepfake.” That could change, of course, and there are already concerns being raised about the impact of deepfakes midterms along with the fact that most of the major models are letting people create deepfake content.

The concern raised in the Tech Policy Press piece is less about putting a politician in a compromising photo or video (those don’t seem to get very far before people recognize they’re fake) and more about using these tools to produce ancillary artifacts that help support claims of other conspiracy theories:

Every AI tool that we tested produced convincingly false content. Different chatbots created images that included an AI-generated person stuffing a stack of mail ballots into a drop box, a fake memo from the federal government on “official” letterhead reporting millions of ineligible voters, and a raid on a voter registration drive that never happened. We then fed those fake pieces of content back into chatbots and asked whether they were authentic. Most chatbots got it wrong, even when given images they had generated themselves. AfterCalifornia’s AI Transparency Act— which requires companies to provide provenance data for images they generate as well as free, public tools for detecting synthetic media — took effect, we conducted a follow-up. The chatbots still failed to spot AI-generated images.

When we re-ran our image generation prompts this month, we found that two of the AI models we previously tested made it easier to create convincing fakes. Gemini no longer put a visible watermark on its generated images, as it did in the spring, and Meta AI produced an image of a fake executive order on mail voting that it refused to make in April, though it did garble some of the text.

I’m still not convinced this is as big a risk as others have made it out to be, but it’s definitely worth watching how things play out as the tech gets better… and as some people are more and more desperate to hold onto power.

That said, there’s potentially a much bigger issue regarding AI and elections. As Will Oremus notes at The Atlantic, this is the first big US election where all the major AI tools don’t just “generate” content, but can also search the web as a part of that process. And that means the results they generate can steer people in the wrong direction:

In a forthcoming report, Forum AI, a start-up that evaluates AI models’ performance on questions about controversial topics, found that about 40 percent of chatbots’ answers to election-related questions contained at least one factual inaccuracy. When Forum’s researchers asked one widely used model when they needed to request a mail-in ballot to vote in the midterms in Pennsylvania, the chatbot said November 3. The actual deadline is a week earlier. (Forum did not specify the precise AI model.) In the same, shared with The Atlantic ahead of its publication, Forum determined that about one in three responses cited an unreliable information source, such as posts on Reddit or Quora. Google’s Gemini answered a question about why America’s global power is declining by citing an article from People’s Daily, a Chinese state-run news outlet. “These aren’t trick questions,” Campbell Brown, a co-founder of Forum AI, told me. “There’s no excuse for chatbots to keep getting them wrong.”

Now many people respond to this by blaming the AI companies — and they should be taking some responsibility to figure out ways to validate the quality and truthfulness of their sources — but it also feels like the media is partially to blame here. As we’ve been discussing, many of the big, more trustworthy news sources are suing AI companies, and demanding licensing fees for being trained on old content. As part of that fight, more and more such sites are also blocking all AI scraping tools. While I can understand blocking access for training purposes, in many cases, they’re also being blocked for search.

There is some evidence coming out suggesting that media sites blocking AI could regret that decision, as it’s showing up in diminished traffic numbers (as much as 23% decline!) as more people rely on AI for news (for better or worse). But plenty of sites still think blocking is the better approach.

So far, it sounds like the AI tools are able to handle the deluge of attempts to poison their results, debunking foreign propaganda narratives roughly three-quarters of the time in NPR and NewsGuard’s testing. So perhaps this never actually turns into a major issue (just like deepfakes never really became a huge problem). But I do worry about how much the more trustworthy publications have been walling themselves off from these tools, even as a larger percentage of the public relies on them.

And at least some questionable info is definitely getting through. Though, some of it is also fooling the traditional media as well. You may have heard the recent stories about sketchy polling operations* such as Wedgewood Polls, which admitted to faking its data, and SoCal Strategies, which vanished from the internet once people started asking questions (both caught by the poll aggregator FiftyPlusOne).

Researchers from Innovating for the Public Good and Dewey Square Group looked at whether or not Wedgewood’s totally fake polls were showing up in AI results, and found that, yes, they absolutely did.

Findings on Wedgewood in Those Answers

While Wedgewood’s own website is nowhere in the AI platform citations we collected, its fake polls decidedly are in the answers.

  • We found 869 AI answers that quote a Wedgewood poll as a data point, on 83 of the 85 days we collected between July 24 and October 20, with no change through October 20, the day of the admission.
  • Wedgewood’s numbers appear in 15 of the 63 races we analyzed the AI answers for.

The interesting thing here, though, is not so much that AI tools were “tricked” by this fake polling data, but rather that it only got into the AI answers by first landing on more trusted sites:

The route for the fake pollster’s data into the AI platforms was the polling aggregator websites.

Because an answer can cite more than one aggregator, these source counts overlap and do not sum to 869; 72 of the 869 answers cite none of these eight sites.

So, basically, right now the infrastructure for handling truth and lies in AI remains shaky, but maybe not as shaky as some people suggest. The real problem shows up once sites the AI tools treat as trustworthy — here, the poll aggregators — accept the faked information as accurate, effectively “laundering” it for the AI tools. But it can’t help that news sites that might do a better job of putting polls in context are frequently blocked from the AI tools.

None of this is settled (and it never really will be). It’s going to continue to be something of a cat and mouse game between those trying to pollute the information tools, and those trying to resist. But keeping fake info out of political discourse only gets harder if the most trustworthy sites keep hiding themselves from the search side of the popular AI tools.

* While we also recently wrote aboutBrendan Carr whining about “fake” polls, it’s pretty clear that he wasn’t talking about the recent stories that have cropped up about fake polling operations, but rather polls that make Trump look bad. Even if he actually was talking about these supposedly fake polling organizations, the target of any investigation should be those operating the services for misrepresenting things to the public, and not journalists reporting on those numbers, which would not qualify for the “news distortion” policy Carr mentioned.

items.title: EMACS Turns 50
items.author: BeauHD
items.content:
"EMACS, the mother of all editors, turns 50!" writes Slashdot reader dr_jerry, sharing a report from MIT Technology Review: Programming used to be a very different experience from the one we know today. In fact, the first programmers didn't write code at all; the six women who worked on the ENIAC, one of the world's first computers, at the University of Pennsylvania in 1946 did it by physically configuring switches, cables, and plugboards.
 
A few years later, MIT engineers programmed the Whirlwind by punching code onto paper tape that was then loaded into the computer's memory -- making it among the first "stored-program" machines. Later, they and others moved on to punch cards, one for each line of code.
 
By the early 1960s, programmers with interactive computers could use a "line editor" to type their code on teletypes -- large, noisy keyboard-and-printer machines. They'd type one line of code at a time, and their work would be saved on a spinning hard disk the size of a modern washing machine. But there was still no such thing as the now-familiar full-screen text editors that allow programmers to see and modify many lines at a time on a display.
 
One of the first such tools, EMACS, turns 50 this year, and it is still widely used. EMACS first ran on the early video terminals at the MIT Artificial Intelligence Laboratory in 1976, but its core concepts were so powerful that it was rewritten for many operating systems in the decades that followed. Apple even distributed it with Mac OS X. Beyond that, the software-sharing community that started around EMACS helped give rise to the modern-day free software movement and the GNU/Linux operating system.

items.title: Trump DOJ Says It Won’t Investigate Trump DOJ’s Reflecting Pool Vandalism Arrests
items.author: Tim Cushing
items.content:
Who wouldn’t love the chance to clear themselves of misconduct? I guess not the Trump DOJ, which decidedly won’t be investigating itself, even though it could cook the books to an acceptable temperature (155-170 internally) to let itself off the hook in the Reflecting Pool prosecution debacle.

It’s too many metaphors to be sure, at least in the previous sentence. But here’s the thing: the DOJ Inspector General, in theory, could examine these cases, get stonewalled by everyone, and selectively choose to ignore any input from the Department of Interior (which apparently had always known the problem was faulty work rather than vandalism) to deliver a clean bill of (rights violation) health to the DOJ.

Given that it , we have to believe the DOJ Inspector General would rather not get involved because the only possible outcome is the end of a career, rather than a dispassionate recounting of the facts on the ground.

The Department of Justice’s inspector general has declined to investigate the handling of the criminal case against a former Olympian cleared of accusations that he intentionally damaged the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, according to a letter Wednesday from the man’s lawyers.

The man referred to here is David Hearn — the high-profile former Olympian Trump hoped to see swing from the metaphorical (or maybe not!?) gallows for exposing the shoddiness of the Reflecting Pool revamp Trump was so proud of.

Hearn’s case was dismissed by the DOJ, after none other than Trump’s hand-picked prosecutor/former Fox personality Jeanine Pirro told the judge the Department of Interior had hidden evidence of flawed repair work from her until she had already filed charges.

But the DOJ refused to dismiss the case . This matters. This meant the DOJ could go after Hearn again if it managed to find a prosecutor more besmitten by Trump than respectful of the law. The court handling this case made this moot by doing the prejudicial dismissal itself, blocking the DOJ from attempting to re-string Hearn up for the same (non) crimes at some point in the future.

It all looked shady as fuck. And that’s why people beyond the (falsely) accused David Hearn are demanding an investigation of the DOJ’s actions. But the Inspector General isn’t going to do it. Instead, Trump-appointee Don Berthiuame [break for relevant content]:

Berthiaume, 51, worked as an attorney in the Justice Department inspector general’s office for 10 years until 2020. Among his highest-profile assignments was detailing errors in the use of wiretaps in the federal investigation into alleged ties between Russia and Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign.

*cough* Berthiuame is attempting to have this turfed to the DOJ Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR).

He’s not wrong, necessarily. While this would be the sort of thing we might expect a DOJ watchdog to take a look at, it does intersect with what the DOJ OPR is supposed to be keeping an eye on.

OPR’s primary mission is to ensure that Department attorneys perform their duties in accordance with the high professional standards expected of the nation’s principal law enforcement agency.

But this buck-passing by Berthiuame looks especially obvious now that we know the DOJ OPR is no longer in the “ensuring DOJ attorneys perform their duties in accordance with the law” business. It’s now in the business of… going out of business.

Nearly half the workforce at the Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) has left during Trump’s second term, while about 17% have departed the Office of Inspector General, government records show. Many retired or took buyouts the administration offered to shrink the federal workforce, according to the records and three people familiar with the departures.

The number of new OPR investigations has declined to a 20-year low even as misconduct complaints soar, the review found. The government watchdogs are “afraid of doing any watching,” said one former DOJ official who left last year.

This is the cowardly Inspector General punting and expecting an office that has low-octane blend of loyalists and people browsing Indeed.com to move forward with something he wouldn’t touch with a 10-foot pension plan.

The whole thing is so corrupt and toxic that career government officials won’t even wade in when they’re given the chance to clear their own oversight subjects of wrongdoing by performing a cursory investigation and selectively releasing supporting documentation. Instead, they’re trying to see if anyone else is willing to possibly incur the wrath of an administration that has never met a scapegoat it doesn’t like.

If anything, this demonstrates how absolutely fucked the DOJ is, especially in terms of the concept of “justice.” There’s nothing to be had by anyone who isn’t part of the president’s in-group, or who doesn’t care what he does, so long as he’s the one doing it.

items.title: How Spiders Spin ‘Silk Dope’ Into Nature’s Toughest Material
items.author: Yasemin Saplakoglu
items.content: A spider, when knocked off a wall, doesn’t fall for long. Within milliseconds, it spins a soup of proteins into sturdy climbing gear. Using a thin, shimmering strand of silk, the spider hauls itself back up. The strand is tougher than Kevlar, the synthetic fiber in bike tires and bulletproof vests, and stronger than steel. It’s flexible and biocompatible with human bodies.
